Context Session Librarian

A local tool for finding, forking and transferring coding-agent sessions.

A useful conversation contains more than its last answer. It records decisions, discarded approaches, tool results and the reasons a project ended up where it did. CSL helps you find that conversation and continue working from its native history.

You can reopen a Codex session, make an independent working copy, or hand a snapshot to another person. Native transfers support Codex and Claude Code. An explicit, experimental conversion path also moves supported history between the two CLIs.

CSL works with local JSONL records. It does not host your conversations or ask you to create another account. The receiving CLI uses its own authentication, configuration and tools.

Install CSL · Read an executed example · User guide

CSL 0.2.2 is published. Read the end of long conversations, find inherited evidence in copies, and choose scrub-all during secret review. Installation now shows its version and helps identify another csl on your PATH. See the release notes for changes and upgrade guidance.

Getting started

You need Linux, Git and Python 3.11 or later. The core uses the Python standard library; there is no pip install or virtual environment to set up. Run the following in the directory where you keep your tools:

Install the published v0.2.2 release
git clone --branch v0.2.2 https://github.com/vitral-ai/context-session-librarian.git
cd context-session-librarian
git checkout --detach v0.2.2
./install.sh

# If ~/.local/bin is not already on PATH:
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
csl --version

This installs the published v0.2.2 tag. Keep the checkout: the installed launcher points to it. To follow ongoing development instead, use git switch main and git pull --ff-only in a clean checkout. Reopening a session requires the corresponding CLI and your own login. GitHub CLI is needed for the optional team exchange and encrypted backup; local library and ZIP transfers work without it. Installing CSL does not activate backups or timers.

For command-by-command options, see the command reference. Team installation covers shared use.

Finding and reading a session

Find a Codex conversation by words you remember, then inspect the messages and evidence behind it. Replace SESSION_UUID with an ID from the search results and use a topic from your own work:

csl index
csl search "database migration" --show-hits --limit 5
csl show SESSION_UUID --tail 10 --include-assistant
csl why SESSION_UUID "database migration"

show --tail N reads the last N messages from the full conversation, after filtering roles. Add --reverse to read that selection newest first; omit --include-assistant for user messages only. The count is messages, not exchanges.

When you inspect a particular copy or fork with why, matching inherited evidence is included and labeled. Global searches reduce duplicate inherited results. To search tool output, use words from the result and add --type tool_result; that flag selects a category, not a literal search word.

Search is lexical, not embedding-based semantic search. Read the matching evidence before deciding which instruction is current. Claude currently has basic discovery through csl sessions --provider claude, rather than the complete Codex library command set. See the command reference.

Passing work on

For regular team handoffs, CSL exchanges snapshots through an existing private GitHub repository, separate from this public source-code repository. Each person needs GitHub CLI authenticated with their own account and access to that exchange. On the sending computer:

csl team connect OWNER/PRIVATE-EXCHANGE
csl sessions --provider codex
csl share SESSION_UUID --title "Database migration handoff"

Connection output points to local sessions to send and an inbox to receive. Run csl index if the local Codex list is empty or outdated. Publishing needs write access; read-only participants can receive.

On the receiving computer, connect to the same exchange and use the actual share ID from the inbox:

csl team connect OWNER/PRIVATE-EXCHANGE
csl inbox
csl receive SHARE_ID --cwd ~/work/project --open

Import creates a new session identity and leaves the source intact. Receiving the same share again reuses its local copy unless you explicitly request another. This is a snapshot handoff, not live synchronization or merging.

If you prefer a file handoff without GitHub, export a local ZIP and send it through a channel you choose. The recipient inspects the received file before importing:

# Sender: creates a local file, without uploading it
csl export SESSION_UUID --to ~/Downloads/handoff.csl.zip

# Recipient: use the received file and an existing project directory
csl import ~/Downloads/handoff.csl.zip --list
csl import ~/Downloads/handoff.csl.zip --cwd ~/work/project --open

A ZIP is a local snapshot, not encrypted backup. Packages contain supported conversation records and embedded assets; they do not copy project files, installed tools, credential files or external attachments. Read transfers and team sharing for details.

Working forks

Create a separate line of work from an existing Codex conversation without modifying the original:

csl native-clone SESSION_UUID --name "New investigation"
# Open the new UUID using the command CSL prints.

Clones receive a fresh UUID. For background agent work, --visibility agent keeps the new copy outside the default interactive picker; an archived snapshot is another explicit option. Visibility is presentation, not access control or filesystem isolation. CSL does not automatically delete copies.

Encrypted backup

Experimental manual backup for Linux/Codex preserves session checkpoints in encrypted containers in an existing private GitHub repository. Incremental runs capture changes; recovery uses a separately retained external key. This is distinct from sending a ZIP or sharing one conversation.

Backup requires GitHub CLI, an explicitly installed age 1.3.2 and operational plus external recovery recipients. Keep the recovery identity outside the source computer. It backs up supported session history, not your repositories, credentials or complete development environment. There are no automatic timers or retention cleanup in this release.

Before updating CSL, finish pending backup runs and recipient-change plans with their original version. The next backup after an update captures local conversations again; older checkpoints still need their original recovery keys. Follow the setup and recovery manual before enabling backup.

Moving between CLIs

Native handoffs keep the same CLI format. Cross-CLI conversion is a separate, explicit operation through the versioned csl-conversation format:

csl convert SESSION_UUID --to claude --cwd ~/work/project
csl receive SHARE_ID --target codex --cwd ~/work/project --open

Conversion supports a bounded profile of text, completed tools, references, embedded images and PDFs. Media conversion needs an optional isolated decoder. Unsupported or inconsistent state can be rejected; CSL does not silently promise to recover an entire opaque checkpoint.

Current scope at a glance
OperationScope
Native ZIP and team transfersCodex and Claude Code
Indexed search and evidence recallCodex; not the full Claude library
Native working forksCodex; experimental native format
Manual encrypted backupLinux/Codex; experimental, optional age and private GitHub required
Cross-CLI conversionExplicit and experimental in both directions
Embedded image and PDF conversionSupported profile; optional decoder required

In CSL, --provider selects or asserts the source CLI; it does not request conversion. Use --target or --to for that. The release's provider matrix and conversion contract describe the full boundaries.

A worked example

This example was run with a synthetic conversation. An early draft used cobalt and Postgres; a later instruction changed that to amber42 and SQLite. A historical tool result contained a third fact, DEMO-617. The continuation question asked for the latest decisions and that tool-only fact without supplying the answers.

The example exports and inspects a ZIP, imports a new identity, and converts a Claude fixture to Codex. Two real Codex continuations then recovered all three facts. You can read the recorded steps below. These are results from an executed fixture, not a terminal running in this page.

Recorded evidence (JSON) · Reproduction script

What these checks establish

The offline run checks source hashes, package checksums, fresh identities and preservation of the selected history. The recorded November 2 live example used Codex 0.166.0 and gpt-6.1-sol, with tools disabled. Both continuations passed. This is evidence for the tested fixture and configuration, not universal compatibility or a new live test of every later commit.

The script defaults to offline operation and uses temporary homes. Run it against the pinned checkout with python3 csl-demo.py --repo /path/to/checkout --out demo.json. Paid reproduction is a separate explicit option.

Native loading and model recall are different checks

A structural check can show that a package is well formed. A native loader check can show that a CLI reconstructs a request from it. A real continuation adds evidence that a model can use the history. None of those alone guarantees that every session fits every model’s context window. The live verification documentation records the broader test method and historical results.

Limits and privacy

Review conversation contents before sharing them. Tool output and ordinary messages can contain credentials or other private information, even when no credential files are collected. Private GitHub access and checksums do not remove that information.

Export and share review readable text for possible secrets before producing a package. Keep or scrub individual findings, cancel, or choose scrub-all for every detected value in the current review. It asks before overriding earlier keep decisions. Source files stay unchanged; this choice does not apply to future operations. For unattended use, choose an explicit policy such as --scrub-secrets.

Detection is partial. Binary attachments, opaque state and values outside the recognized patterns need separate review. A successful scan does not certify that a conversation is safe to share. Scrubbing changes the exported copy, not the source history.

CSL does not copy authentication or translate permissions between tools. Imported instructions are historical context, not new authority to execute a task. Account access, model availability and the behavior of future CLI versions remain outside the transfer’s guarantees.

The project

CSL is a project by Vitral. It grew out of the practical need to locate and hand over useful agent conversations. The tool can be used independently of Vitral’s workspace product.

CSL is licensed under Apache-2.0, with Vitral attribution. The published version is v0.2.2, with experimental manual encrypted backup. Versions v0.1.1 and v0.1.0 remain available unchanged.

Contributions should start with a reproducible problem, synthetic history and a focused change. Reports about a real workflow are useful; please do not post private conversation exports or credentials in public issues. The issue tracker is the place for public bug reports and proposals.

Codex and Claude Code are products of their respective owners. Their software, services and marks are not licensed by the CSL project.
